content.prompt: Identify events as independent or dependent.

inlines.text: Tossing a coin then tossing another.

answer.worked: The first coin toss does not change the probabilities for the second toss.

inlines.text: Rolling a die then rolling another.

answer.worked: The first die roll does not change the probabilities for the second roll.

inlines.text: Picking a card from a deck, then picking another one without replacing it.

answer.worked: The first card is not replaced, so the remaining deck and the probabilities for the second selection change.

inlines.text: Picking a card from a deck, replacing it, then picking another card after shuffling.

answer.worked: Replacing the card and shuffling restores the original selection probabilities.

inlines.text: Tossing a coin then rolling a die.

answer.worked: The coin toss does not change the probabilities for the die roll.

inlines.text: Choosing a marble from a jar, replacing it, shaking the jar, then choosing another.

answer.worked: Replacing the marble and mixing the jar restores the original selection probabilities.

inlines.text: Choosing a chocolate from a box, eating it, then choosing another.

answer.worked: Eating the first chocolate removes it from the box, changing the possibilities for the second selection.

inlines.text: Choosing a marble from a jar, without replacing it, then choosing another marble.

answer.worked: The first marble is not replaced, changing the contents of the jar and the probabilities for the second selection.
Replacement restores the original contents, so the probabilities for the next random selection remain unchanged.
Without replacement, the first selection changes the remaining contents and the probabilities for the next selection.

content.prompt: Identify these events as independent or dependent.

inlines.text: You roll a six-sided die and then flip a fair coin.

answer.worked: The result of the die roll does not change the probabilities for the coin flip.

inlines.text: You have a bag with red marbles and blue marbles. You draw a marble, note its color, and then draw another marble without replacement.

answer.worked: Without replacement, the first marble changes the numbers of red and blue marbles remaining, so the probabilities for the second draw change.

inlines.text: You draw a card from a standard deck and record its suit. You replace the card and shuffle the deck, then draw a second card from the deck.

answer.worked: Replacing the card restores the original deck. After shuffling, the probabilities for the second card's suit are unchanged by the first draw.

inlines.text: You have a drawer with black socks and white socks. You select a sock, record its color, and then select another sock without replacement.

answer.worked: Removing the first sock changes the numbers of black and white socks remaining, so the probabilities for the second selection change.

inlines.text: You check the weather forecast in the morning, and based on that information, you decide whether to bring an umbrella.

answer.worked: The decision to bring an umbrella depends on the information in the weather forecast.

teachingContext.taughtMethod: Independent events have unchanged probabilities after previous results; dependent events have probabilities affected by previous results. Replacement restores the original collection.

inlines.text: A fair coin is tossed nine times and comes up heads each time. What is the probability it will be heads on the tenth toss? Why?

answer.worked: The coin is fair, so $P(\text{heads})=\frac{1}{2}$. Coin tosses are independent, so the first nine results do not change the probability on the tenth toss.

teachingContext.taughtMethod: Independent events have probabilities unaffected by previous results; successive coin tosses are independent.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain how replacement affects independence and how the first colour determines the remaining jellybean.

inlines.text: A bag contains a red jellybean and a blue jellybean.
Scenario 1: A jellybean is drawn randomly, the colour recorded, and then returned to the bag. Afterwards, a second jellybean is drawn.
Scenario 2: A jellybean is drawn randomly, the colour recorded, and it is then eaten. Afterwards, a second jellybean is drawn.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Out of the two scenarios, which one represents a series of independent events, and which one represents a series of dependent events?

answer.short: Scenario 1 is independent; Scenario 2 is dependent.
answer.worked: Scenario 1 is independent because replacing the first jellybean leaves the bag unchanged. Scenario 2 is dependent because eating the first jellybean changes what remains in the bag.

children.label: b
children.prompt: In scenario 1, explain why the probability that the second jellybean is red is $\frac{1}{2}$, regardless of the colour of the first jellybean.

answer.short: Replacement leaves one red and one blue jellybean, so the draws are independent and $P(\text{second red})=\frac{1}{2}$.
answer.worked: The first jellybean is returned, so the bag again contains one red and one blue jellybean. Therefore $P(\text{second red})=\frac{1}{2}$ regardless of the first colour; the draws are independent.

children.label: c
children.prompt: In scenario 2, explain why the conditional probability of the second jellybean being red, given the colour of the first jellybean, is not $\frac{1}{2}$.

answer.short: If the first is red, the probability is $0$; if the first is blue, the probability is $1$.
answer.worked: If the first jellybean is red, only the blue jellybean remains, so $P(\text{second red}\mid\text{first red})=0$. If the first jellybean is blue, only the red jellybean remains, so $P(\text{second red}\mid\text{first blue})=1$.

teachingContext.taughtMethod: Replacement leaves successive draws independent; without replacement, the first result changes the probabilities for the second draw.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain how replacement affects independence and how the first colour determines the remaining jellybean.

content.prompt: Two four-sided dice are rolled and then their results are added.

inlines.text: Complete the table to list all outcomes.

answer.worked: Each cell is the sum of its row and column headers. The rows are $2,3,4,5$; $3,4,5,6$; $4,5,6,7$; and $5,6,7,8$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of outcomes}&=4\times4\\&=16\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: What is the probability that the dice sum is 4?

answer.worked:
The three outcomes giving a sum of 4 are $(1,3)$, $(2,2)$ and $(3,1)$.
$$P(\text{sum is }4)=\frac{3}{16}$$

inlines.text: What is the probability that the dice sum is 5 or greater?

answer.worked:
There are $4+3+2+1=10$ cells with sums of 5, 6, 7 or 8.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{sum is }5\text{ or greater})&=\frac{10}{16}\\&=\frac{5}{8}\end{aligned}$$

sourceReview.taughtMethod: Add the two dice results in each table cell; check the total using the fundamental counting principle; count favourable cells and divide by the total.

inlines.text: A six-sided die is rolled twice.

children.prompt: How many possible outcomes are there?

answer.worked: There are 6 rows of 6 outcomes: $6\times6=36$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the probability of rolling a double?

answer.worked: The 6 diagonal cells are doubles. $$P(\text{double})=\frac6{36}=\frac16.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: What is the probability of not rolling a double?

answer.worked: There are $36-6=30$ cells that are not doubles. $$P(\text{not a double})=\frac{30}{36}=\frac56.$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: What is the probability of rolling a 2 and a 3, in any order?

answer.worked: The favourable outcomes are $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$. $$P(\text{2 and 3 in any order})=\frac2{36}=\frac1{18}.$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: What is the probability of rolling two odd numbers?

answer.worked: The odd rows and columns are 1, 3 and 5, giving $3\times3=9$ favourable cells. $$P(\text{two odd numbers})=\frac9{36}=\frac14.$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: What is the probability of rolling a sum of 5?

answer.worked: The favourable outcomes are $(1,4)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,2)$ and $(4,1)$. $$P(\text{sum of 5})=\frac4{36}=\frac19.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Neither bulb is faulty.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}P(\text{neither faulty})&=\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{4}\\P(\text{neither faulty})&=\frac{3}{10}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: First bulb is faulty and the second not.

answer.worked:
Let $F$ mean faulty and $N$ mean not faulty; the letters give the selection order.
$$\begin{align*}P(FN)&=\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{3}{4}\\P(FN)&=\frac{3}{10}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: The second bulb is faulty and the first is not.

answer.worked:
Let $F$ mean faulty and $N$ mean not faulty; the letters give the selection order.
$$\begin{align*}P(NF)&=\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{4}\\P(NF)&=\frac{3}{10}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Exactly one of the bulbs is faulty.

answer.worked:
The faulty bulb can be selected first or second. These outcomes are mutually exclusive.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{exactly one faulty})&=\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{4}\\P(\text{exactly one faulty})&=\frac{3}{10}+\frac{3}{10}\\P(\text{exactly one faulty})&=\frac{3}{5}\end{align*}$$

children.label: f

answer.worked:
The complement is that neither bulb is faulty.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{at least one faulty})&=1-P(\text{neither faulty})\\P(\text{at least one faulty})&=1-\frac{3}{10}\\P(\text{at least one faulty})&=\frac{7}{10}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Find the probability she passes only one of the exams.

answer.worked:
Assuming the test results are independent, the maths pass/fail branches have probabilities $0.8$ and $0.2$. The science pass/fail branches have probabilities $0.6$ and $0.4$ after either maths result.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{maths pass, science fail})&=0.8\times0.4=0.32\\P(\text{maths fail, science pass})&=0.2\times0.6=0.12\\P(\text{only one pass})&=0.32+0.12\\&=0.44=44\%\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Find the probability she passes at least one of the exams.

answer.worked:
Assuming the test results are independent, the complementary event is failing both tests.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{both fails})&=0.2\times0.4=0.08\\P(\text{at least one pass})&=1-P(\text{both fails})\\&=1-0.08\\&=0.92=92\%\end{align*}$$

Let $B$ denote black and $W$ denote white. The first-stage probabilities are $\frac{4}{12}$ and $\frac{8}{12}$. After a black counter, the second-stage probabilities are $\frac{3}{11}$ and $\frac{8}{11}$; after a white counter, they are $\frac{4}{11}$ and $\frac{7}{11}$.

children.prompt: Find the probability that Hannah selects at least one white counter.

No white counters means two black counters.
$$\begin{align*}P(BB)&=\frac{4}{12}\times\frac{3}{11}=\frac{12}{132}\\P(\text{at least one white})&=1-P(BB)\\P(\text{at least one white})&=1-\frac{12}{132}=\frac{120}{132}=\frac{10}{11}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a

answer.worked:
Let $S$ denote a six and $N$ denote a number other than six.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{exactly 1 six})&=P(SN)+P(NS)\\P(\text{exactly 1 six})&=\frac16\times\frac56+\frac56\times\frac16\\P(\text{exactly 1 six})&=\frac{10}{36}\\P(\text{exactly 1 six})&=\frac5{18}\end{align*}$$

answer.short: $HHH,\ HHT,\ HTH,\ HTT,\ THH,\ THT,\ TTH,\ TTT$; $P(\text{at least 1 head})=\frac78$.
answer.worked:
The ordered outcomes are $HHH,\ HHT,\ HTH,\ HTT,\ THH,\ THT,\ TTH,\ TTT$. Seven of the eight equally likely outcomes contain at least one head.
$$P(\text{at least 1 head})=\frac78.$$

children.prompt: How could you use complementary events to calculate the answer to part d quickly?

answer.worked:
The complement of at least one head is no heads, which means all tails.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{at least 1 head})&=1-P(\text{no heads})\\P(\text{at least 1 head})&=1-P(\text{all tails})\\P(\text{at least 1 head})&=1-\frac12\times\frac12\times\frac12\\P(\text{at least 1 head})&=\frac78\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: A deck of 52 playing cards contains 12 picture cards.
Two cards from the deck are drawn at random and placed on a table.
What is the probability, correct to four decimal places, that exactly one picture card is on the table?

answer.worked:
There are $52-12=40$ non-picture cards. Exactly one picture card can occur in either order.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{exactly one picture card})&=\frac{12}{52}\times\frac{40}{51}+\frac{40}{52}\times\frac{12}{51}\\&=\frac{960}{2652}\\&=\frac{80}{221}\\&\approx0.3620\end{align*}$$

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · variation-sequence · pf-8e8a6f6fed]
Idea: Vary the number of spins while keeping the spinner fixed to expose how additional opportunities change the probability of at least one red.

Proposed addition: Under p29-b add the single instruction: 'Predict how the probability of at least one red changes as the number of spins increases.' Ask for the probability of at least one red in (i) 1 spin, (ii) 2 spins, (iii) 3 spins and (iv) 4 spins, retaining the existing three-spin calculation as (iii). Answers: 1/4, 7/16, 37/64, 175/256. entries.description: Independent and Dependent Events

Multistage Experiments
A multistage experiment consists of two or more steps.
For example:
• rolling two dice
• flipping three coins
• flipping a coin, then rolling a die, then picking a card from a deck.

Independent and Dependent Events
An independent event doesn't change based on previous results.
Example: Flipping a coin twice - the second flip doesn't depend on the first.
A dependent event changes based on previous results.
Example: Taking two marbles from a bag - the second pick depends on the first.

entries.description: Multiplication Rule

Multiplication Rule for Multistage Experiments
If two successive events A and B in a multistage experiment are independent, then:
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
We can write P(A and B) as P(AB) and P(A, B) and P(A ∩ B).
Note that P(A and B) is not always equal to P(B and A) for multistage probability.

entries.description: Calculate the probability of a player winning the game.
Calculate the probability that a player will lose at least once in two consecutive games.
How many games must be played before you have a 90% chance of winning at least one game? (hint: set up an equation and use logarithms)
A two-way table is useful for this question
entries.expectedAnswer:
a. P(win) = 16/36 = 4/9
b. P(lose at least once in 2 games) = 1 − P(win both)
= 1 − (4/9)^2 = 1 − 16/81 = 65/81
c. P(win at least once in n games) ≥ 0.9
1 − (5/9)^n ≥ 0.9
(5/9)^n ≤ 0.1
n ≥ log_(5/9)(0.1) ≥ 3.917 …
∴ 4 games or more
entries.presentation: Supplied blue working, right-aligned beneath the question. No two-way table is actually supplied.

entries.description: Probability Trees with Dependent Events

• Dependent events occur when there is no replacement.

   b. Use 1 − P(none) when the question asks for “at least one.”
The probabilities on any pair of branches should sum to 1.
All final events should sum to 1.

entries.description:
HSC Advanced Sample Question Band 5
A box contains n marbles, of which k marbles are coloured red and the remainder of the marbles are coloured green. Two marbles are drawn randomly from the box.
If the first marble is not replaced into the box before the second marble is drawn, then the probability that the two marbles drawn are the same colour is:

presentation.heading: Bold black, unbanded question heading
presentation.sourceOrder: Heading, prompt, options A–D; supplied solution beside and below options
presentation.responseSpace: Open working space below the question; dimensions uncertain

entries.description: Supplied blue two-stage probability tree. First-stage outcomes, top to bottom: R and G. Each has second-stage outcomes R above G. Visible branch probabilities: first R, k/n; first G, (n-k)/n; R then R, (k-1)/(n-1); G then G, (n-k-1)/(n-1). The R then G and G then R branches have no printed probability labels.

presentation.role: Supplied answer diagram, separate from the unsolved student prompt
presentation.orientation: Left-to-right stages; R above G at each split
presentation.houseStyle: Editable tree with black ordinary strokes and complete labels at 10 pt final size

entries.description:

∴ P(same colour) = k/n · (k-1)/(n-1) + (n-k)/n · (n-k-1)/(n-1)
= [k(k-1) + (n-k)(n-k-1)]/[n(n-1)]
Supplied choice: D.

presentation.alignment: Second line aligned at the equals sign
